# Documenting your code

You already keep a notebook for this course, with your lab work and your plans. In this tutorial, you also use it for your analysis: the commands you run, why you run them, and what you see. You hand in your notebook before your presentation, and your teachers read it to prepare their questions. One part of your grade is about how well you document your work.

Good notes also help you. A command that makes sense today can be a mystery in a few weeks. With clear notes, you, a fellow student or your teachers can see what you did and why, and run it again.


## What the tutorial asks you to write down

From the HPC chapter on, blue notebook boxes tell you what to add to your notebook. Step by step, you build up these habits:

- A comment above each command: what it does, and if it is not obvious, why
- Where your data came from, and when you got it
- A check after each step that makes or changes files, for example with `ls` or `wc -l`
- One sentence after each number or figure: what it means for your data
- Your choices, and why you made them, for example the cutoffs for quality filtering
- Once you work on the HPC: where each command ran, with `# On my computer` or `# On Crunchomics`

Some boxes ask you to add these sections to your notebook:

- `## Software`: the tools you used, their versions, and where they came from. This goes near the top
- `## Error log`: the errors you got, and how you fixed them
- `## Questions`: anything that is still unclear


## Code blocks in your notebook

Your notebook is a Quarto (`.qmd`) or R Markdown (`.Rmd`) file. In both, a code block starts and ends with three backticks. What you write right after the first three backticks decides what happens to the code:

```` markdown
```bash
# This block is only shown. It is not run.
ls data
```

```{{bash}}
# This block is run when you render your notebook.
ls data
```

```{{r}}
# This R block is also run when you render your notebook.
1 + 1
```
````

For the commands from this tutorial, always use ```` ```bash ````, without curly brackets. These commands run on Crunchomics, in a project folder that does not exist on your own computer. In a ```` ```{bash} ```` block, your notebook would try to run them on your computer when you render it, and stop with an error.

Use ```` ```{r} ```` for R code that you run yourself, for example when you analyse your count table.


## Markdown basics

The text around your code blocks is written in Markdown. These are the basics you need most:

| You type | You get |
|---|---|
| `# Heading`, `## Smaller heading` | headings (leave a space after the `#`) |
| `- item` at the start of a line | a bullet point |
| `1. item` at the start of a line | a numbered list |
| `**bold**`, `*italic*` | **bold**, *italic* |
| `` `ls -l` `` | `ls -l`, for a command or file name inside a sentence |
| `[link text](https://quarto.org)` | a link |
| `![](path/to/figure.png)` | a figure |

Leave an empty line before a heading, a list and a code block. Otherwise, Markdown may not recognise them.

Notice that `#` means something different in two places. In normal text, it starts a heading. Inside a code block, it starts a comment.

[Markdown Basics](https://quarto.org/docs/authoring/markdown-basics.html) on the Quarto website lists everything else you can do with Markdown.


## An example notebook

To see what a notebook for this kind of analysis can look like, have a look at [my notebook for the analysis of last year's student data](https://ndombrowski.github.io/MicEco_teaching_material/source/miceco_analysis.html). The [Quarto file behind it](https://github.com/ndombrowski/MicEco_teaching_material/blob/main/source/miceco_analysis.qmd) is on GitHub.

This notebook is my own working record of the analysis of last year's student data. It uses the same steps as this tutorial, but runs them on all samples and goes further, so it also shows checks, side tracks and dead ends. Your notebook does not need to be this long. It shows what a notebook can look like once an analysis grows.

Things to look for:

- A short project description at the top
- The software, with versions
- Comments above the commands, and notes on the results between the code blocks

My notebook uses another way to keep the bash code from running: a setting at the top of the file (`eval: false`). For your notebook, ```` ```bash ```` is simpler.


## Further reading

- [A Guide to Reproducible Code in Ecology and Evolution](https://assets.britishecologicalsociety.org/2017/12/guide-to-reproducible-code.pdf) from the British Ecological Society: how to organise project folders and write code that others can run again. The examples are mostly in R, but the advice applies to bash too
